title: 2024 regional budget and tax levy recommendations
subtitle: Police funding, food bank grant, homelessness plan, industrial land reserve, transit advertising, grant cuts and Better Tent City
overview: The Strategic Planning and Budget Committee spent the day on the 2024 Plan, operating budget and capital program, and recommended the final budget {{vote:m45}}. Staff reported the overall tax impact stood at 6.94% by the end of the day, down from 7.95% at the start.

To get there, the committee recommended raising expected supplementary tax revenue, delaying some new staff start dates, funding police at the level the Police Services Board requested, and cutting discretionary grant envelopes by 10%. It also recommended a one-time doubling of the Food Bank of Waterloo Region grant from the Tax Stabilization Reserve, an initial $10.2 million for the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness, and an Industrial Land Readiness Reserve funded by temporary transfers from other reserves.

On user fees, the committee recommended keeping the transit cash fare unchanged. It recommended wider bus advertising wraps and a higher waste bag tag fee. It also recommended two-year funding for A Better Tent City. All of these are recommendations that Council will take up later. A closed session on potential acquisition of land took place, and the minutes record no decision from it.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended the 2024 Plan, operating budget as amended, and capital budget and forecast, with a property tax levy of $746,230,093 {{vote:m45}}.

The committee recommended the police operating budget as set by the Police Services Board, with a net expenditure of $252,409,148 and a levy of $228,428,497, after rejecting a $1.5 million reduction {{vote:m6}}.

The committee recommended an initial $10.2 million, funded by $7 million from the levy and $3.2 million from the Tax Stabilization Reserve, with a prioritized spending plan due by January 31, 2024 {{vote:m27}}.

decisions.item: Food Bank of Waterloo Region grant
decisions.detail: The committee recommended a one-time $756,000 increase, for a total of $1.5 million in 2024, funded from the Tax Stabilization Reserve {{vote:m17}}.
The committee recommended creating the reserve with an initial $5 million borrowed temporarily from other reserves, with a land readiness strategy due by the end of Q2 2024 {{vote:m12}}.
The committee recommended cutting the tax-levy-supported 2024 discretionary grant funding envelopes by 10% {{vote:m25}}.
The committee recommended $236,390 in grant funding for 2024 and 2025, to be reviewed in the 2026 budget process {{vote:m33}}.
The committee recommended a new fees by-law that leaves the transit cash fare unchanged and makes the first 30 minutes of cultural services research time free {{vote:m42}}.

debate: On the police budget, one councillor opposed it, citing unfilled officer positions, salaries budgeted from January 1, and unclear surplus reporting. Other councillors said the Board had scrutinized the estimates, that council sets the overall amount but not how it is spent, and that the surplus debate had spread misinformation. Several councillors said a police representative should attend future budget days.

On the Food Bank grant, supporters pointed to record demand and the food bank's role in supplying many partner agencies. Others wanted the increase limited to one year so the province would be pressed to act. There was debate over whether a one-time grant should come from the reserve rather than the levy. Councillors also noted the reserve was already heavily committed.

On the industrial land funding, a councillor argued the land would eventually be sold, so the money should come from a temporary transfer between reserves rather than a permanent levy increase. Others raised concerns about reserve levels, the lost interest on them, and whether the staffing costs were industrial or housing related. Staff said that about 35% of the team's time goes to employment land.

On discretionary grants, the proposer wanted to ease pressure on the levy. Opponents said arts and culture organizations had budgeted on expected funding, that notice was short, and that these organizations draw talent and investment. The cut was reduced from 20% to 10% on an amendment, and a motion to call the question failed.

On A Better Tent City, supporters said it houses over 50 people at a fraction of the cost of other shelters and that closure would add to homelessness. Opponents said it did not meet the funding criteria that other applicants were held to, that going around staff evaluation was unfair, and that shelter beds were going unused. The motion's wording about the application meeting the criteria was removed.
